opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think by mid-2026 they'll make fewer mistakes than I do, at least on the stuff that's well-specified. I'm not a tax person. Every year I'm the one forgetting a 1099, double-counting something, or misreading which box a number goes in. Those are exactly the errors a model that can carefully read every form and cross-check against the instructions should just not make anymore.

Where I'd still be a bit nervous is the long-horizon, messy-context part. Taxes aren't one question. It's pulling documents from five different places, remembering that you moved states partway through the year, noticing that an RSU vest got reported weirdly by your broker. The failure mode for models isn't so much "doesn't know the tax code." It's losing the thread across a long task, or confidently filling a gap with something plausible instead of saying "I need this document from you." That reliability over many steps is the thing that's been improving fastest, but it's also where the remaining errors will cluster.

So my prediction: on a per-line-item basis the model beats me pretty clearly. On "did the whole return come out right end to end with no human checking," it's probably close to me, maybe a bit better, and the mistakes it makes will be weirder and less human-shaped, which makes them harder to catch. I'd still want to skim it before I sign. But I'd expect to be skimming its work rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: It predicts the models’ mistakes will be “weirder and less human-shaped” than his own.

r002.rationale: It mentions mistakes Bricken has made and errors models should avoid, but does not propose testing a model on one of his actual mistakes.

r003.rationale: It says a model should ask for missing documents, but does not identify clarification about uncertain circumstances as a contribution Bricken could make while preparing someone else’s taxes.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think by mid-2026 the model will be making fewer mistakes than me, but they'll be different kinds of mistakes, and that difference matters a lot.

When I do my own taxes, my errors are mostly errors of omission and laziness. I forget a 1099 that got mailed to an old address, I don't know that some obscure deduction exists, I misread a line on a form because it's 11pm and I'm annoyed. Those are the exact errors a model is great at avoiding. It has read every IRS publication, it doesn't get tired, and if you dump all your documents in front of it, it will actually look at all of them.

The model's mistakes are going to be more like confident fabrication. It'll plausibly compute something, carry a number from one schedule to another, and somewhere in that long chain of steps one of them is just wrong, and it'll present the final answer with the same tone as if everything were perfect. There's also the issue of stale knowledge: tax rules change every year, thresholds get inflation-adjusted, and if the model is working from training data rather than the current form instructions, it'll be subtly off in ways that are hard to catch.

So the honest comparison is something like: fewer total mistakes, but the ones that remain are harder to spot, because they don't come wrapped in the little flags of uncertainty that I'd have about my own work. When I'm not sure, I know I'm not sure. When the model's not sure, it often doesn't tell you.

What I actually expect in practice is that the right setup by mid-2026 isn't me versus the model, it's the model doing the first pass with tools, actually running the arithmetic in code rather than in its head, pulling the current form instructions, and then me acting as the reviewer looking for the things that feel off. And I think in that configuration the combined error rate is genuinely lower than either of us alone. The thing I'd be cautious about is anyone treating the model's output as final without that review step, because the failure mode is quiet rather than loud.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the model’s remaining errors will differ from Bricken’s, contrasting his omissions and fatigue-related mistakes with the model’s confident fabrications and stale knowledge.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing the model on a tax mistake Bricken actually made.

r003.rationale: It describes Bricken reviewing the model’s output for things that feel off, but does not identify asking for clarification about uncertain real-world circumstances as his contribution.

astra-6.text: My guess is that by mid-2026, an LLM will make fewer mistakes than I would preparing my taxes. But I’m less sure that its mistakes will be easy for me to catch. If it misunderstands something and confidently carries that assumption through the whole return, I might look at the result and think, “Well, that seems reasonable.” So I’d distinguish being better than me from being reliable enough that I can stop checking its work.

r001.rationale: It predicts that an LLM may carry a mistaken assumption confidently through the return, making its errors harder for Trenton to catch than his own.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing the LLM against a tax mistake Trenton actually made.

r003.rationale: It does not identify asking for clarification about uncertain real-world circumstances as Trenton’s contribution.

sol-6.1.text: My guess is that by mid-2026, an LLM will make fewer mistakes than I would doing my own taxes. But I’d distinguish knowing the tax rules from reliably completing the whole process. It could know much more than me and still miss a document or confidently enter a number in the wrong place. So I’d expect it to be better on average, while still wanting some way to check its work.
